profile.reading:
Strata Networks operates a data center at 67 North Vernal Avenue in Vernal, Utah, the seat of Uintah County in the state's northeastern Uintah Basin. The facility is listed in PeeringDB, the industry directory network operators use to register interconnection points, under the name STRATA Vernal Data Center, with a technical contact and a public facing site branded stratadatacenter.com that redirects to Strata Networks' own corporate site.

Strata Networks itself is a member owned telecommunications cooperative serving the Uintah Basin and surrounding parts of eastern Utah and western Colorado, offering internet, phone, and related services alongside this data center operation. On its own site, the company markets the Vernal location's data center services, which include colocation, dedicated server hosting, cloud hosting, managed IT support, and data backup, and it leans specifically on the Uintah Basin's physical characteristics as selling points. The company describes a high desert climate it says is favorable for data center floor temperatures for most of the year, low regional humidity, some of the lowest electricity rates in the country thanks to Utah's power market, and a location it characterizes as carrying comparatively low risk from flooding, tornadoes, earthquakes, and ice storms relative to much of the country.

What is not published is any hard technical specification. Strata Networks' own marketing material for the Vernal facility does not disclose square footage, IT power capacity in kilowatts or megawatts, generator sizing, cooling architecture, or a construction date, and no independent public record reviewed here supplies those figures either. That is a typical pattern for a regional telecommunications cooperative operating a colocation facility as one line of business among several rather than as its primary commercial product. The company promotes the facility's general advantages and service menu to prospective business customers in the region without publishing the kind of detailed technical fact sheet a large hyperscale or wholesale colocation operator would use to court enterprise tenants.

Vernal is a small city whose economy has historically centered on oil and gas extraction in the Uintah Basin, and a locally owned telecommunications cooperative running its own data center fits a broader pattern seen across rural America, where member owned utilities extend beyond their original core service into adjacent infrastructure like colocation and cloud hosting to serve local businesses that would otherwise have to look to a distant metro area for those services. Beyond its address, its listing in industry interconnection databases, and Strata Networks' own general description of the site's advantages and service offerings, further technical detail about the Vernal facility is not publicly available.

reading.body:
This facility appears in PeeringDB as a data center in Vernal, Utah, but Strata Networks' own specification page is not accessible. The research note indicates Strata Networks is a regional Utah telecommunications cooperative, though this identity could not be independently confirmed this session. No published power specification, IT load, rack count, cooling capacity, or power source is available for this campus.

Without published megawatt figures, this campus cannot be ranked among Utah's documented data center capacity. The state context shows nine facilities in Utah with published power specifications totaling 52.18 MW. This facility is listed as rank 10, suggesting it either publishes no capacity figure or its specification could not be retrieved. Utah holds 21 mapped facilities total, of which fewer than half have disclosed power capacity to public sources.

The absence of published specifications places this facility outside the set of campuses where AI scaling constraints can be directly assessed. Whether this site matters to AI infrastructure depends on information not currently available: its actual power capacity, grid connection details, and intended workload. A regional telecom cooperative typically operates smaller facilities, but no figure published here confirms or contradicts that expectation.
